title: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of the post/redirect/get pattern and identify at least two of its listed subtopics.
Trace the worked example for the post/redirect/get pattern and describe its expected result.
Select a focused test or verification step for a normal case and a meaningful failure boundary.

content.intro: Explore the post/redirect/get pattern through the source syllabus topics, a small inspectable example, and a practical verification task. The example is teaching material, not a claim that the platform executed Flask code.
content.why_it_matters: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern matters because it helps a Flask application keep its request/response behavior explicit and testable as the surrounding project grows. Learners should understand the responsibility, when to use it, and its failure boundaries instead of only memorizing an API call.

content_blocks.title: Visual guide: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
content_blocks.alt_text: Post / Redirect / Get: Browser submits POST; Server validates + saves; Server redirects to GET; Browser displays feedback.
content_blocks.caption: PRG reduces accidental resubmission; it does not make a write operation idempotent by itself.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern matters because it helps a Flask application keep its request/response behavior explicit and testable as the surrounding project grows. Learners should understand the responsibility, when to use it, and its failure boundaries instead of only memorizing an API call.

content_blocks.title: What to learn
content_blocks.text: This lesson covers: Why duplicate submissions happen; Redirecting after successful POST requests; User feedback after redirects. Keep the source terms intact; for each one, name the component that owns the behavior, the inputs/assumptions, and the expected result.

items.title: Why duplicate submissions happen
items.text: For why duplicate submissions happen, identify the component responsible, the input it receives, and the observable result it should produce.

items.title: Redirecting after successful POST requests
items.text: Trace which parts of the incoming request are trusted, which are optional, and how invalid data maps to a response.

items.title: User feedback after redirects
items.text: When applying user feedback after redirects, keep the implementation small, document version-dependent behavior, and verify it with a focused check.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
content_blocks.expected_output: A GET request to /users/7 returns JSON similar to {"user_id": 7, "url": "/users/7"}. An invalid or unknown ID can be handled with an HTTP error.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as app.py, run `flask --app app run --debug` locally, and request /users/7. Do not expose the development debugger publicly.

content_blocks.title: Before using this beyond practice
content_blocks.text: Validate untrusted input at the server boundary, keep secrets out of source code, and test the failure path. Optional extensions or hosting infrastructure are separate dependencies unless stated otherwise.

content.expected_result: A GET request to /users/7 returns JSON similar to {"user_id": 7, "url": "/users/7"}. An invalid or unknown ID can be handled with an HTTP error.
content.run_instructions: Save as app.py, run `flask --app app run --debug` locally, and request /users/7. Do not expose the development debugger publicly.
troubleshooting: Confirm the expected virtual environment and installed dependency versions before diagnosing framework behavior.
Check route/method, input shape, status code, traceback location and relevant configuration one at a time.
For database or third-party integration examples, use isolated local resources and explicit timeouts; do not use production credentials.
content.reset_steps: Stop the local development server, reset only disposable local practice data if needed, and remove temporary artifacts created by the exercise. Never delete production data or migration history to reset practice.
content.try_it_yourself: Apply the post/redirect/get pattern to a tiny local Flask app. Predict what a normal request should do, test one invalid or boundary case, and record expected versus observed behavior.
progressive_hints: Name the Flask component or ecosystem tool responsible for the post/redirect/get pattern.
Run the smallest example in an isolated local project and compare the actual response with the stated expected result.
Add one negative or boundary test, then check the linked version-specific official documentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a fragment without checking its imports, app configuration or dependencies.
common_mistakes.why: Many Flask examples assume a configured app and a specific runtime or extension version.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the run instructions, record the Flask/Python version and test the smallest behavior first.

common_mistakes.problem: Checking only the successful request path.
common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, unsupported methods, unauthorized objects and service failures often have different behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a negative or boundary test and assert the status code and response contract.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a local example as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Secret management, concurrency, deployment, monitoring and failure recovery need separate design decisions.
common_mistakes.fix: Review the matching deployment and security references before publication or real use.

content.recap: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern connects Why duplicate submissions happen; Redirecting after successful POST requests; User feedback after redirects. Verify the example under the selected environment and keep its assumptions visible.
content.accessibility_notes: Use descriptive headings, meaningful labels and alt text; provide a text explanation of the diagram; keep code selectable and keyboard navigable; never rely on color alone.
content.version_notes: Baseline: Flask 3.1.x, with the official changelog listing 3.1.3 on 2026-02-18. Verify current patch versions and ecosystem compatibility before use. Optional packages are not Flask built-ins.
content.task: Apply the post/redirect/get pattern to a tiny local Flask app. Predict what a normal request should do, test one invalid or boundary case, and record expected versus observed behavior.

hints: Identify the main responsibility behind the post/redirect/get pattern.
Keep request/data boundaries explicit and verify assumptions with a focused test.

content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: trace one input through the relevant framework component, keep validation and authorization explicit, and write the smallest test that demonstrates the intended behavior. This note does not claim the example was executed.
summary: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern is part of static assets and html forms and should be understood alongside its listed source subtopics.
The worked example is a focused fragment; use the stated context and dependencies before running it.
Verify expected and failure behavior locally and record the check so it can be reproduced.
